2. The appellant in Civil Appeal No.18 of 1997 filed writ petition No.5321 of 1996 seeking declaration that the Act was void, illegal, ultra vires of the Constitution and of no legal effect and further that Dhanmondi PS Case No.10(10) of 1996 dated 2-10-96 and Lalbagh PS Case No. 11(11)/1975 dated 14-11-1975 were unlawful and void. 

 6. The constitutionality of the Act has been challenged from various standpoints which will be noticed in course of the following discussion. 

 11. The aforesaid criminal case under sections 120B/302/149/34/307/109 of the Penal Code was started in connection with the occurrence of the 15th August, 1975 which is against the provision of the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 and paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule as aforesaid. The Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 by which the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 has been repealed is illegal, void and ultra vires of the Constitution. 

 13. The High Court Division took up the writ petitions together for consideration as the issue in both the petitions was the same, rather one. Mr. Md Korban Ali, learned Counsel for the appellants before us, himself appeared for the writ-petitioners while the learned Attorney-General represented the Government respondent. It appears that on the request made by the court six senior members of the Bar had also appeared and made their submissions as Amicus Curiae there was also an intervener at the end. The High Court Division copiously recorded the submissions of all the learned counsels, whatever was argued, in the impugned judgment. The most striking feature of this laboriously written long judgment which is bound to attract anybody's attention is the lengthy submissions made by almost all the learned Counsels including the learned Attorney-General (except Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and of course the Counsel of the appellants) to the effect that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was itself a void legislation. The High Court Division found all the reasoning in support of the said submission to be acceptable and accordingly held: 

 "Considering the above, we hold that the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is void under Articles 7(2) and 26(2) of the Constitution. As we are declaring this Ordinance No.50 of 1975 void, it had and has no legal existence in the eye of the Constitution on the very day when it was promulgated that is on 26-9-75 and now". 

 "So, it appears to us that a void law though not declared void by any Court so long was legally repealed by the Parliament and, as such, there was no illegality or unconstitutionality in passing the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996" 

 (3) It is held that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance 50 of 1975) is void since it is repugnant to the Constitution. 

 (5) It is found that the five out of six learned jurists of the country (excepting Mr. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed) who assisted the Court as Amicus Curiae, expressed their views that the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 is a valid piece of legislation and the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 is void being ultra vires the Constitution Submissions of the learned Attorney-General and the views of the majority Amiei Curiae on the points of validity of the Indemnity (Repeal) Act No.21 of 1996 and the repugnancy of the Indemnity Ordinance No.50 of 1975 appear to be constitutionally and legally correct and, as such, the same are accepted. 

 15. We have noticed that a substantial part of the judgment of the High Court Division, rather the major part, has been devoted to the consideration of the submission made on behalf of the Government and supported by all the Amici Curiae except one that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was a void legislation and the submission has been accepted. The Indemnity Ordinance has been declared void. Apart from the question of correctness and propriety of the decision, we have failed to understand why the vires of the said Ordinance was made the major issue for decision when none of parties came to the Court seeking a declaration that the Ordinance was ultra vires. On the other hand, the question directly rose for consideration and decision by the writ-petitioners was whether the Indemnity (Repeal) Act. 1996 was ultra vires. That was the only constitutional question for decision before the High Court Division. 

 17. So the effect of a law is that as if it never existed and it is obliterated completely from the records of the Parliament except for the purpose of those actions which were taken under it. That being the position in law, the Indemnity Ordinance was not in existence after the passing of the Repeal Act and it was therefore unthinkable, in our opinion, to declare the Ordinance void which was not even in existence. It was, so to say, a contradiction in terms. 

 18. Then again, why should the Government or anybody else consider itself or himself wiser than the Parliament? When the Parliament decided to repeal the Indemnity Ordinance, it must be presumed that the Parliament had recognized the Ordinance to be a valid and existing law. Otherwise there would have been no necessity for repealing the Ordinance. If the Parliament considered the Ordinance to be void, it could have passed a declaratory legislation to that effect instead of repealing it. The learned Attorney-General leading the argument that the Ordinance was void had unwittingly put the legislature, as it appears, to embarrassment in that the Repeal Act was proved to be unnecessary. 

 19. Then again, the High Court Division having itself found that the Indemnity Ordinance was a continuing law after withdrawal of martial law being protected and saved under paragraphs 3A and 18 of the Fourth Schedule and further having itself noticed that despite the ouster of jurisdiction of Court it can consider the constitutional validity of any law only if the same is found to be made without jurisdiction, Coram non juices or malafide, it is not understood how the High Court Division could declare the Ordinance to be void on the ground that it was repugnant to the Constitution. 

 20. Except on grounds of jurisdiction, etc. as above all laws made during the period between the 15 August, 1975 and the 9th April, 1970 "shall not be called in question in or before any Court, tribunal or authority on any ground whatsoever" Para 18. The High Court Division accepted this position and yet declared the Ordinance to be void without explaining as to how the bar of jurisdiction was overcome by it. 

 21. In any view of the matter, it appears that the finding made by the High Court Division, which appears to be the main burden of its judgment, that the Indemnity Ordinance was void is an uncalled for gratuitous finding and, as such, the same cannot be supported. 

 39. Mr. Korban Ali raised the question of malafide also because the criminal cases were started even before the repeal of the Indemnity Ordinance. It has been noticed that in such matters what is of importance is the authority to act and not with -What motive the action is taken. It could not be said that the alleged bar under the Indemnity Ordinance was attracted automatically as soon as the FIR was lodged. It has/had to be pleaded at some stage. Since the Ordinance has already been repealed, the bar does no longer operate and no question of malafide can be raised in opposition to the proceedings. 

 42. The lopsided pre-occupation of the learned Judges of the High Court Division with the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 being void ab initio, leaves me with a finding that the following matters remain completely unanswered by them and also by the learned Attorney-General while defending the impugned judgment before us. 

 43. First, it was open to any citizen to ask for a declaration from the High Court Division in the writ jurisdiction that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was void ab initio No person has ever done it at any point of time during the 21 years that the said Ordinance was in operation. The said Ordinance was repealed on the 14th November, 1996 by the Parliament passing by a simple majority the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996. The writ petitioner-appellants challenged the constitutional validity of the Repeal Act of 1996 in their respective writ petitions. The Government-respondents put up as defence that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 was void ab initio. They did not and indeed could not have sought for a declaration as respondents in the two writ petitions that the said Ordinance was void ab initio. Yet the High Court Division gave in favour of the respondents an unsolicited and uncalled for declaration that the said Ordinance was void ab initio. It is as if a plaintiff in a suit had asked for a declaration of title to the suit land, but obtained instead a declaration that he is the illegitimate son of his father. The High Court Division may or may not have accepted the soundness of the respondents' defence but it could not have given a declaration to that effect in the writ petitions filed by the appellants challenging the validity of another Act. It is not permissible in a writ petition to give a declaration in favour of the respondents because it is the writ petitioners who are seekers of a declaration, not the respondents. No one had the boldness to challenge the said Ordinance frontally in a writ petition for such a declaration. If the High Court Division can take such an unusual step it will set up a dangerous precedent. 

 44. Secondly, Parliament has already acted earlier on November 14, 1996 repealing the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. The High Court Division could not have declared the same Ordinance as void ab initio at a later date on 28-1-97. This is like killing a mocking bird twice. To declare a statute as void when it is already repealed is to kill a dead horsetwice. Also it means in effect that the exercise of the Parliament was an exercise in futility and that the Repeal Act, 1996 was absolutely unnecessary. Can the High Court Division ascribe futility to the legislative activities of the Parliament and give a parallel and competing decision of its own when the issues involved could be decided on other points conclusively? For it is a cardinal principle of interpretation of statutes that no statute or part of it will be declared unconstitutional or void if the issues involved in a case can be decided otherwise. 

 45. Thirdly, the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 has suffered two different fates in the hands of two organs of the State—Parliament has repealed it and the High Court Division has declared it void ab initio. A statute cannot be repealed and void declared a b initio at the same time, because the effect of repeal and the effect of such a declaration are different. The learned Chief Justice has quoted Crazies on Statute Law (Seventh Edition) at p.351 as to the effect of a repeal. When an Act of Parliament is repealed it must be considered (except as to transactions past and closed) as if it had never existed. But repeal is always relatable to an existing law and a valid law. In Black's Law Dictionary (Fifth Edition) at p.1167 "Repeal" is defined as follows: 

 46. Therefore only an existing law can be repealed but if a Court declares a statute void ab initio then the effect is that the statute did not exist at all in the statute-book. It was never an existing law at any point of time. There can be no transaction under a void statute. The question of past and closed transactions does not arise in the case of void statutes. When a statute is repealed by Parliament section 6 of the General Clauses Act comes in aid in preserving and continuing vested rights, privileges, obligations or liabilities acquired, accrued or incurred under the repealed enactment, unless a different intention appears in the repealing statute. In the Repeal Act, 1996 this different intention has been expressed in section 2 of the Act by doing away with past actions, measures taken, certificates or orders or instructions given, etc. under the repealed Ordinance. If section 2 was not there, which it was the option of the Parliament not to incorporate, all the actions, certificates granted, advantages gained, if any, under the repealed Ordinance would have had a continuing force. Further, a statute is repealed prospectively or retrospectively according as the tenor of the repealing statute is. In the present case the Repeal Act, 1996 repealed the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 prospectively (এতদ্বারা রহিত করা হইল). It means it was an existing law till the 13th November, 1996. When a statute is repealed by the Parliament its disappearance from the statute-book takes place from the date of repeal, either prospectively or retrospectively according as the legislature prescribes. But if a statute is declared void ab initio by the Court its disappearance from the statute-book takes place retrospectively from the date of enactment of the repealed statute, never prospectively. If a statute is declared void ab initio by a Court no rights accrue at all. No obligation or liability generates from the void law. But a repealed statute retains accrued rights and obligations, unless avoided specifically or by necessary implication. The High Court Division did not keep in mind this vital distinction between a repeal of a statute and declaration of a statute as void ab initio and therefore put itself into the pitfall of committing a constitutional fallacy, expressing unnecessarily, a separate intention of its own than that of the Parliament which had already repealed the statute. 

 47. Fourthly, a void statute may be avoided in two ways, as rightly argued by one of the Amicus Curiae before the High Court Division, namely, by approaching the Court for a declaration that the statute is void ab initio or by the Parliament itself passing a declaratory statute. As already noticed no one has ever approached the Court for a declaration of that kind. The Parliament did not pass a declaratory statute either. The High Court Division wrongly held "a void law though not declared void so long by any Court was legally repealed by the Parliament". Again the High Court Division made a confusion between repeal and enactment of a declaratory statue. 

 49. In the present case no Court of law has earlier pronounced that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 is void ab initio. The Parliament was therefore free to pass a declaratory statute declaring that the said Ordinance was void from the very beginning, but it did not do so. It preferred to treat the said Ordinance as an existing law and repealed it. The High Court Division made a basic mistake in holding that the Parliament has legally repealed a void law, little giving thought that a void law has to be declared void by a declaratory statute and a repeal can only be made of an existing law. 

 50. Fifthly, in case of repeal the Repeal Act is itself liable to be repealed by the same Parliament or subsequent Parliament, reviving the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975, but when a Court declares the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 void ab initio the Parliament cannot re-enact the same legislation afresh. It will be struck down as unconstitutional. It is buried forever. This distinction was lost sight of by the High Court Division. 

 (1) Why Indemnity (Repeal Act, 1996 should not be declared as void, illegal, ultra vires of the Constitution and of no legal effect. 

 (2) Declare the Dhanmondi PS Case No. 10(10)96 dated 2-10-96 and Lalbagh PS Case No.11(11)75 dated 4-11-75 as unlawful and void. 

 64. In the judgment of the High Court Division, the main thrust was with regard to the constitutionality of the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975. It appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that the learned Advocates of the appellants and the respondent as well as the Amicus Curiae appearing in this case mainly argued with regard to the constitutionality of the Ordinance itself. After consideration of the submissions of the learned Advocates the learned Judges held that the Ordinance is ultra vires of the Constitution and consequently declared the same as void as if, it had no legal existence in the eye of Constitution on the very day when it was promulgated and thereafter. Consequently, the learned Judges in the ordering portion in Item No. 3 held as follows: 

 "It is held that the Indemnity Ordinance, 1975 (Ordinance No. 50 of 1975) is void since it is repugnant to the Constitution." 

 It may be stated that in both the writ petitions no challenge was made in respect of the Ordinance itself rather it was the case of the writ petitioners that the Indemnity (Repeal) Act, 1996 is void, illegal, ultra vires of the Constitution and is of no legal effect. The Repealing Act was under challenge and not the original Ordinance. In that view of the matter, on the averments in the writ petitions the declaration with regard to the Ordinance itself was un-called for within the frame of the writ petitions when the Ordinance itself was not the subject matter of challenge before the High Court Division. The Repealing Act being under challenge the learned Judges of the High Court Division was under an obligation to decide the validity of the Repealing Act itself, but unfortunately the learned Judges travelled beyond their lawful limits and unnecessarily decided that issue which was not necessary to decide in this case at all. The whole exercise should have been in a narrow compass as to the constitutionality of the repealing Act.
